title: TempFlow-GRPO: Knowing When Each Step Matters
one_liner: When training a model to draw pictures humans prefer, reward early decisions more because they shape the whole image, not equally like today's methods do.
lead: Flow models draw images one noisy step at a time, gradually removing blur until a clear picture emerges. Standard reinforcement learning (learning by reward) treats all steps the same, even though early steps pick the big structure and later steps just add details. TempFlow-GRPO finds which steps matter most and focuses learning effort there, training 10 times faster because every training update improves decisions that actually shape the outcome, not wasted on steps that barely change anything.

problem.h2: Every step looks the same to today's methods
paras: An image generator works like an artist revealing a painting under a thick fog. At first, you can only see shadows and rough shapes (big structure). Halfway through, the fog lifts and you see major colors and layouts. By the end, only fine details remain. Each step of this process is different in how much it shapes the final picture.

Today's methods treat all steps equally: they give each step the same learning signal when a human likes the final result. This is like paying an artist the same for deciding the composition as for adding a few brush strokes. The big decisions get lost in the noise. Early steps (which determine whether it looks like a cat or a dog) and late steps (which add whiskers) get the same learning signal, so the model wastes training effort on learning to fine-tune early-stage details instead of on perfecting structure—the learning signal cannot distinguish which decisions actually shaped the outcome because all steps are weighted equally.

A beginner might try: 'Just add a tiny reward at each step so learning spreads out.' This fails because you cannot know in advance what small rewards to use, and even if learning spreads to all steps equally, each step's nudge toward correctness is wasted if that step barely affects the final image—like trying to steer a car by adjusting the mirror angle and the steering wheel equally.

callout.html: Track which steps actually affect the outcome most by testing steps in isolation, then weight learning stronger for high-impact steps.

steps.text: Run the model once with random (random) noise injected at only timestep k, compare final image to baseline, measure how reward changed.
Test noise at step 0, then step 1, then step 2, etc. Record how much each step's randomness shifted the final reward.
Steps that moved the reward most get higher learning weights. Steps that moved it barely get low weights.

During reinforcement learning, multiply each timestep's learning signal by its weight so important steps get stronger training nudges—the model learns to refine structure-shaping steps because those are where learning actually sticks and moves the reward.
Use the same random initializations across tests to isolate the true effect of each timestep without confounding randomness.

paras: The paper changes how the learning signal (gradient) is distributed across timesteps. Instead of sending the same learning signal to all steps, it sends stronger signals to early steps (where one pixel choice cascades into big changes because the entire rest of the image is built on top of it) and weaker signals to later steps (where choices have already solidified from earlier steps and cannot be undone).

hidden.name: How much each step shapes the outcome
paras: This is the hidden quantity: for each step in the generation process, how much does changing that step actually change the final image quality score? Early steps that determine shape and color have high criticality. Late steps adding texture have low criticality.

The paper measures it by switching a timestep from smooth denoising to noisy denoising in isolation, then recording how much the final reward shifted. If switching step 1 to noisy changes reward by 5 points but switching step 7 changes it by 0.1 points, step 1 has much higher criticality. The paper uses these measured criticalities as weights during training.

heat.caption: Darker means higher criticality. Early steps are highlighted because they shape more. White steps barely affect outcomes.

reads.html: Think of building a house: deciding the foundation matters enormously; repainting the front door matters less. The foundation has high criticality.
The paper isolates each step by applying random denoising only at that step, keeping other steps smooth, then measures reward variance as the criticality metric.

mechanism.h2: Why focusing on critical steps speeds up learning
paras: Here is the core: a flow model draws an image by removing blur step by step. Early steps carve out big shapes (a head, arms, background). Late steps just refine texture. When humans score the final image, they score based on whether it looks right overall, not whether the last texture is perfect. So early decisions influence the score much more than late ones.

Standard learning spreads the reward signal equally to all steps: each step gets nudged the same amount. But most of that nudge at late steps is wasted—those decisions barely affect the score, so the learning cannot stick. It is like trying to teach someone by giving identical feedback for critical choices and trivial ones.

TempFlow-GRPO measures how much each step actually moves the score (by testing in isolation). Then it weights the learning signal: steps that move the score a lot get strong training nudges; steps that barely move it get weak nudges. Early steps now absorb most of the learning effort, where it counts. The model converges faster because every learning step improves something that matters.

stages.s: Measure each timestep's impact on final score
Assign learning weights: high for early, low for late
Model converges to human-preferred style in 10x fewer steps

math.words: For each timestep, multiply the learning update by a weight proportional to how much noise at that timestep moves the final reward.
math.equation: L = sum_t w_t * loss_t, where w_t is proportional to std(reward | noise at t)
symbols: total learning loss for this batch
add up the loss from all timesteps
how wrong the model is at timestep t
how much the final reward changes when you add randomness only at timestep t (the measured criticality)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Test 1: Add noise at step 0 (early structure decision). Final reward ranges 18-22 across runs. Standard deviation = 2.0.
Test 2: Add noise at step 5 (mid texture). Final reward ranges 19.9-20.1. Standard deviation = 0.1.
Weights: w_0 = proportional to 2.0 = 2.0 relative units. w_5 = proportional to 0.1 = 0.1 relative units. After normalizing: w_0 = 20x, w_5 = 1x.
During training, step 0 gradients are multiplied by 20, step 5 gradients by 1. Step 0 receives 20x stronger training signal because it actually moves the outcome.

math.note: The weight is the measured impact: steps that wiggle outcomes a lot when perturbed get higher multipliers, so learning focuses where it matters.

charts.title: Standard GRPO (uniform weights)
charts.note: Learning spreads evenly across steps. Progress is slow because most effort goes to late-stage tweaks that barely affect outcomes.

charts.title: TempFlow-GRPO (critical-step weights)
charts.note: Learning concentrates on early steps so every update improves high-impact decisions. Convergence is 3x faster because step 100 of weighted training beats step 300 of uniform training—the same human time invested teaches more when nudges go toward choices that actually move the score.

items.html: If you use different random starting noise for each branching test, you cannot tell if reward changed because of the timestep or because of the seed. Fix: hold seeds constant across all impact measurements.
If late steps have near-zero impact, their weights become tiny. The model stops learning to refine them at all. Fix: enforce a minimum weight so even low-impact steps get some training signal.
If the model is random (random), testing a single branching point gives noisy numbers. You measure criticality incorrectly if you only test once. Fix: average over many branching trials per timestep.

Use the same batch of random seeds for all impact tests, run many trials per timestep, compute standard deviation carefully, then normalize weights to have mean 1 so the overall learning rate stays sane.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny flow model (say, generating 32x32 images of simple shapes). Train it with a basic reward (e.g., how well the shape matches a target outline). First run standard GRPO with uniform weights across all steps. Plot training loss over 500 steps. Then run TempFlow-GRPO: measure step criticalities by isolating each step and checking reward variance, assign weights, retrain. Plot this on the same graph.
demo.closing: TempFlow-GRPO should reach the final quality in roughly one-third the steps (or fewer). The graph shows an unmistakable knee bend where the weighted version pulls away from uniform.
